name: Reduction of the Coast (Siletz) Reservation by the Act of March 3, 1875 (Royce areas 578 and 579)
aka: Alsea and Siletz reservations, Act of March 3, 1875
Coast Reservation set apart by Executive Order of November 9, 1855
citation: Act of March 3, 1875, 18 Stat. 446 (Royce schedule p. 878); the reservation itself was set apart by Executive Order of November 9, 1855
nations: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians (Alsea, Yaquina, Coos, Lower Umpqua, Siuslaw, Tillamook, Tututni, Coquille, Chetco and other peoples then on the Coast Reservation)
promises: Not a treaty. The Executive Order of November 9, 1855 set apart the Coast Reservation for the Indians on the coast of Oregon, from the mouth of the Tsiltcoos River north to a point due east of Cape Lookout (Royce, p. 814).
Royce's own entry for the 1855 order points to this queue entry's areas: 'Another portion relinquished by act of Congress, Mar. 3, 1875. See 578, 579, 479' (Royce, p. 815).

The 1875 Act restored a portion of the Alsea and Siletz reservation to the public domain (area 578) and kept a smaller tract, from two miles south of the Siletz agency north to the Salmon River, 'as a permanent reservation' for the Indians (area 579) (Royce, p. 878).
The Siletz Tribe records that Senator Mitchell added a proviso that the Act would not take effect unless the Indians in the areas to be opened agreed to remove (CTSI).

breaches.what: Congress removed a large part of the Coast Reservation, including the Alsea reservation, and opened it to non-Indian settlement; the Supreme Court later described the Act as removing additional land from the reservation in order to open more land for public settlement.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Act of March 3, 1875, 18 Stat. 446, as described in United States v. Alcea Band of Tillamooks, 329 U.S. 40 (1946)

source.title: United States v. Alcea Band of Tillamooks, 329 U.S. 40 (1946)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.quote: in order to open more land for public settlement, removed additional land from the reservation

breaches.what: The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians say the Act opened about 700,000 more acres of their reservation to non-Indians, that the Yachats headmen repeatedly said they wanted to stay, that a former agent falsely reported their consent to remove, and that about 225,000 acres remained.

source.title: Changing Federal Policy & Reduction of the Coast Reservation by Act of Congress, 1875

landTaken: The Siletz Tribe gives about 700,000 acres opened by the 1875 Act and about 225,000 acres remaining afterward (CTSI). Royce gives no acreage for areas 578 and 579.
compensation: No payment for the land removed in 1875 was found. Alcea (1946) held four tribes entitled to compensation for their original title under the jurisdictional act of August 26, 1935; Docket 239 (1955) notes the Court of Claims valued the Alcea lands as of 1855 at $1.20 per acre (115 Ct. Cl. 463, 1950).
today: The tract kept in 1875 (area 579) was itself reduced by the agreement of October 31, 1892, ratified August 15, 1894 (28 Stat. 286), ceding the unallotted land for $142,600.00; in Docket 239 the Indian Claims Commission found that price an unconscionable consideration for land it valued at $575,396.00 (findings of November 23, 1955). That cession is the separate queue entry cession-1894-08-15-indians-on-coast-of-oregon.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the 1875 Act took most of what was left of its reservation for settlers, on a report of consent that its headmen never gave.

openQuestions: treaties.json dates this entry 1855-11-09 and names it for the 1855 order, but its Royce areas 578 and 579 are the March 3, 1875 entry on Royce p. 878; the 1855 order itself is the separate file cession-1855-11-09-indians-on-coast-of-oregon. Not edited.
The text of 18 Stat. 446 was not opened directly (the govinfo link for that page redirected); the Act is cited through Royce, Alcea (1946) and the Docket 239 findings.
Area 579 is the tract the Act kept as a permanent reservation, not a taking in 1875; it is the land later ceded in 1892.

Whether any court or the Indian Claims Commission awarded compensation specifically for the 1875 removal (for example to the Alsea, Coos, Lower Umpqua or Siuslaw) was not settled; Coos Bay Indian Tribe v. United States (1938) and Siletz claims in later dockets are leads.

The existing file cession-1894-08-15-indians-on-coast-of-oregon is marked contested; the Docket 239 unconscionable-consideration finding (id 466 and opinion id 106) appears to support a broken status there. Reported, not edited.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. An 1855 presidential order set apart the Coast Reservation for the Indians of the Oregon coast. In 1875 Congress kept a smaller tract as a permanent reservation.
plain.happened: Congress in 1875 removed a large part of the reservation, including the Alsea reservation, to open it for settlement, as the Supreme Court later described. The Siletz Tribe says its headmen never consented.
plain.today: No payment for the 1875 removal was found. The tract kept in 1875 was mostly ceded in 1892 for a price the Indian Claims Commission later found unconscionable.
